prompt: Where is the three-bit Ethernet CoS/PCP marking carried?
options: In the priority field of an IEEE 802.1Q tag
In the final three bits of an IPv4 source address
In the complete eight-bit IPv6 Traffic Class field
In the destination port of a UDP transport header
explanation: The 802.1Q tag carries a 3-bit priority code point (CoS/PCP). Untagged Ethernet has no PCP field.

whyWrong.1: An IPv4 source address identifies a host and carries no QoS marking.
whyWrong.2: The IPv6 Traffic Class carries DSCP and ECN, not the Ethernet PCP.
whyWrong.3: A UDP port can be a classification criterion but is not a marking.

prompt: On classic IOS LLQ, why does the priority class have a rate limit during congestion?
options: To hold unused priority capacity idle until more voice arrives.
To bound priority consumption so other classes can receive service.
To set the same maximum rate for all nonpriority classes.
To delay excess priority packets in the congestion-time policer.
explanation: The congestion-time policer caps the priority class so it cannot starve the other classes. Unused priority bandwidth stays available to other traffic.

whyWrong.0: Unused priority capacity is available to other traffic, not held idle.
whyWrong.2: The limit applies only to the priority class, not to all other classes.
whyWrong.3: The policer drops excess priority packets; it does not delay them.

prompt: What is the main purpose of QoS when several applications compete for a busy link?
options: Increase the physical capacity of the contracted circuit.
Remove the propagation delay between the two sites.
Allocate available forwarding service according to the traffic policy.
Reserve the same treatment across every independent provider.
explanation: QoS decides how a congested link's existing capacity is shared among competing traffic. It cannot add capacity or control other providers' networks.

whyWrong.0: QoS allocates existing capacity; it does not increase it.
whyWrong.1: Propagation delay depends on distance and medium, not queuing policy.
whyWrong.3: A local policy does not configure other administrative domains.

prompt: Which action is marking rather than classification?
options: Checking whether an IP packet belongs to the managed-phone subnet.
Writing AF21 into the packet’s DSCP field.
Comparing a packet’s UDP destination with a voice-service port.
Matching a packet against a supported application signature.
explanation: Marking writes a value into a packet field such as DSCP. Classification only decides which traffic category a packet belongs to.

whyWrong.2: Comparing a port number against a criterion is classification.
whyWrong.3: Matching an application signature is classification.

prompt: Which two statements correctly compare policing and shaping? Choose two.
options: A shaper guarantees delivery by allowing an unlimited queue
A policer can remark excess traffic instead of discarding it
A policer lowers the interface's negotiated physical speed
A shaper can buffer excess traffic and add waiting time
A shaper cannot transmit a short burst above its average rate
explanation: A policer applies its configured exceed action, which can be a remark instead of a drop. A shaper buffers excess traffic, which adds delay.

whyWrong.0: A shaper's buffer is finite and drops packets when it fills.
whyWrong.2: A policer limits traffic rate; it does not change the negotiated link speed.
whyWrong.4: A shaper allows short bursts above the average rate by using its burst allowance.

exhibit.title: Representative policer excerpt
exhibit.text:
police cir 1000000
  conform-action transmit
  exceed-action set-dscp-transmit af13
exceeded 1750 packets; actions: set-dscp-transmit

prompt: What happens to the 1,750 packets counted as exceeding this policer?
options: They wait until the policer's dedicated shaping queue drains
They are discarded because all exceed actions mean drop
They receive EF so they can bypass downstream congestion
They are transmitted with AF13 instead of their earlier mark
explanation: The exceed action in the policy is set-dscp-transmit AF13, so excess packets are remarked and forwarded. Only a drop action discards them.

whyWrong.0: A policer has no queue; only a shaper buffers excess traffic.
whyWrong.1: This policer's exceed action is remark-and-transmit, not drop.
whyWrong.2: The action sets AF13 (DSCP 14), not EF.

prompt: In a supporting IOS CBWFQ policy, what does `bandwidth 512` mean for DATA?
options: A minimum 512 kb/s share during congestion, with excess capacity usable
A permanent 512 kb/s ceiling, with all additional packets discarded
A 512-byte queue limit, with later arriving packets tail-dropped
A 512 kb/s physical link speed, negotiated with the neighboring device
explanation: The CBWFQ bandwidth command guarantees a class a minimum share during congestion. The class can use spare capacity.

whyWrong.1: A ceiling needs a policer or shaper; bandwidth is a minimum.
whyWrong.2: The 512 is in kb/s, not a queue length in bytes.
whyWrong.3: Class bandwidth does not set or negotiate the physical link speed.

exhibit.title: Representative classic IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
Class-map: VOICE
  Match: dscp ef (46)
  Priority: 128 (kbps), burst bytes 3200
  b/w exceed drops: 400

prompt: During congestion, this classic IOS LLQ counter increases by 400. What does it identify?
options: The physical interface has dropped to a speed of 128 kb/s
The voice classifier failed to match the arriving packets
The priority class exceeded its permitted rate/burst allowance
The DATA class was capped at its minimum bandwidth
explanation: The bandwidth-exceed counter in an LLQ priority class counts packets its congestion-time policer dropped for exceeding the rate or burst. It does not indicate a speed change.

whyWrong.0: The priority policy does not change the interface speed.
whyWrong.1: The class policer counts packets already matched to the class, so the classifier worked.
whyWrong.3: DATA's minimum bandwidth does not produce this counter.

prompt: Which interpretation of AF32 is correct?
options: DSCP 32; AF class 3 with drop precedence 2
DSCP 28; AF class 3 with drop precedence 2
DSCP 26; AF class 2 with drop precedence 3
DSCP 46; the recommended Expedited Forwarding code
explanation: AFxy equals 8x + 2y, so AF32 is 8×3 + 2×2 = 28: class 3, drop precedence 2.

whyWrong.0: AF32 is a name, not decimal 32.
whyWrong.2: DSCP 26 is AF31; AF32 has class 3, not class 2.
whyWrong.3: EF is DSCP 46, a different code point.

prompt: Many TCP flows slow down together after a full FIFO queue drops a burst. Which mechanism spreads congestion signals earlier across flows?
options: Strict priority for every class on the output interface
Changing all packets to the same AF drop precedence
Random early detection before the queue is completely full
Increasing each endpoint's advertised Ethernet link speed
explanation: RED/WRED drops selected packets before the queue is full, so flows slow at different times instead of all at once. This avoids TCP global synchronization.

whyWrong.0: Strict priority for every class removes differentiation and gives no early drops.
whyWrong.1: Giving all packets the same drop precedence does not create early queue management.
whyWrong.3: Endpoint link speed does not change the bottleneck's capacity.

prompt: Users can set DSCP on their own PCs, but only managed phones should get preferred treatment. Where should markings be validated first?
options: At the destination, after the traffic has already crossed the managed queues.
At the ingress boundary, before received marks select preferred treatment.
At the WAN exit only, while every earlier switch accepts endpoint markings.
At the endpoint itself, treating its self-selected value as authorization.
explanation: Validate or re-mark at the trust boundary, normally the ingress access switch, before untrusted markings select preferred queues. Markings from unmanaged devices must not be trusted.

whyWrong.0: Validation after the managed queues is too late; resources are already consumed.
whyWrong.2: Earlier switches would still honor untrusted marks.
whyWrong.3: A user-set mark must not authorize itself.

prompt: A classifier requires both: source belongs to the managed-phone subnet AND DSCP is EF. A PC outside that subnet sends an EF-marked packet. How is it evaluated?
options: It matches because the EF criterion is sufficient for this rule.
It matches because source membership is checked only after queue selection.
It fails because both criteria are required and source membership fails.
It fails because the policy compares the criteria as an OR expression.
explanation: A match-all rule requires every criterion to be true. The PC's EF mark matches but its source is outside the subnet, so the packet fails.

whyWrong.0: EF alone is not enough when the rule requires both criteria.
whyWrong.1: Both conditions are evaluated during classification.
whyWrong.3: The rule is AND; under OR the EF match would have been enough.

prompt: A 1,500-byte packet is serialized onto a 1 Mb/s link. Ignoring all additional framing overhead, how long does serialization take?
options: 1.5 ms
8 ms
150 ms
12 ms
explanation: Serialization delay = bits ÷ bit rate: 1,500 × 8 = 12,000 bits ÷ 1,000,000 b/s = 12 ms.

whyWrong.1: 8 is the bits-per-byte factor, not a time.
whyWrong.2: 150 ms is the voice delay guideline, not this calculation.

prompt: Two voice paths have the same average one-way delay. One varies between 20 and 100 ms; the other stays near 60 ms. What differs for the playout buffer?
options: The first path has higher physical bandwidth because its minimum is lower.
The second path has higher loss because its packets share similar delay.
The first path must have lower serialization delay on every hop.
The first path has greater delay variation despite the equal average.
explanation: Jitter is variation in delay, and the playout buffer must absorb it. The first path has higher jitter despite the equal average.

whyWrong.0: Delay samples say nothing about physical bandwidth.
whyWrong.1: Stable delay does not mean higher loss.
whyWrong.2: Delay variation does not identify serialization delay on any hop.

prompt: Two policies see the same short burst after the token allowance runs out. One remarks and sends it; the other buffers it until sending is allowed. Which pair matches?
options: The policer forwards with a changed mark; the shaper adds waiting time.
Both hold the excess packets until a dedicated policing queue empties.
Both discard the burst because a rate limit always means drop.
The shaper changes physical link speed; the policer reserves bandwidth.
explanation: A policer takes its configured action (here remark and transmit) with no delay. A shaper holds excess packets in a buffer, which adds waiting time.

whyWrong.1: A policer has no queue for excess traffic.
whyWrong.2: The stated actions are remark and buffer, not drop.
whyWrong.3: Shaping controls departure timing; neither policy changes link speed or reserves bandwidth.

exhibit.title: Observed attachment
exhibit.text:
GigabitEthernet0/1
 Service-policy input: MARK-IN
  Class-map: DEFAULT-IP
   Match: dscp default (0)

prompt: PC-A requests enter Gi0/0 and leave Gi0/1. MARK-IN is applied inbound on Gi0/1, and its counters rise while a ping succeeds. What must you check before concluding the requests are marked?
options: Inspect the request headers and move the policy to their intended ingress.
Raise the marking policy’s rate while leaving its attachment on Gi0/1.
Accept the aggregate match count as verification for both packet directions.
Replace the mark with EF while keeping the Gi0/1 input attachment.
explanation: Replies enter Gi0/1 and increment the counters while requests enter Gi0/0, which has no policy. Check the request headers and attach the policy at Gi0/0 ingress.

whyWrong.1: A higher rate does not move the policy to the requests' ingress port.
whyWrong.2: The counter also counts replies, so it does not verify the requests.
whyWrong.3: A different mark applied at Gi0/1 still misses the requests.

exhibit.title: Authored correlated observations
exhibit.text:
Local router: verified voice classification; priority allowance not exceeded.
Local voice-drop counter unchanged during the complaint.
Capture before/after downstream switch: the same voice stream retains EF.
Downstream shared egress queue: depth rises and drops increase during the complaint.
The downstream class mapping and scheduler have not yet been inspected.

prompt: Local classification is correct and the EF mark arrives intact downstream, yet voice is impaired. What should you check next?
options: Increase the local priority allowance because no local drops prove downstream congestion.
Set every local packet to EF so all flows use the same downstream service.
Inspect the downstream queue policy, competing demand and voice treatment during impairment.
Disable local marking because unchanged EF values prove it is unnecessary.
explanation: A preserved mark does not guarantee per-hop treatment. Check the downstream device's queue policy, class mapping and competing traffic.

whyWrong.0: No local drops does not show where congestion is, and more local priority will not fix a downstream queue.
whyWrong.1: Marking everything EF removes traffic differentiation and does not fix the downstream treatment.
whyWrong.3: The mark is only useful if the downstream policy honors it, so local marking stays.

prompt: Which one-way delay is the voice guideline in the lesson?
options: 150 ms
15 ms
500 ms
explanation: The voice guideline is 150 ms one-way delay, 30 ms jitter and 1% loss.

whyWrong.1: 15 ms is far below the guideline.

prompt: How many bits does the DSCP field use in the IP header?
explanation: DSCP is a 6-bit value in the IP header; the CoS in an 802.1Q tag is 3 bits.

whyWrong.0: Three bits is the 802.1Q CoS/PCP field.
whyWrong.2: Eight bits is the whole ToS/Traffic Class byte, which also holds ECN.
whyWrong.3: No QoS marking field here is 16 bits.

prompt: When does queuing take effect on an interface?
options: Only during congestion
Whenever a packet is forwarded
Only when the link is down
Only for TCP traffic
explanation: Queuing and scheduling matter only when packets compete for a congested interface. On an idle link every packet is sent at once.

whyWrong.1: Packets leave immediately when there is no congestion.
whyWrong.3: Queuing applies to all traffic, not just TCP.

prompt: What is the DSCP value of class selector CS5?
explanation: CSn equals 8n, so CS5 is 40. EF is 46.
